title: Are Brazil's critical minerals next in line for Trump's quest to commandeer resources?
gist: The Trump administration has used Pentagon industrial-policy vehicles to take equity-like stakes plus long-term offtake in Venezuelan oil (roughly 20% of proven reserves, 100-year concession) and in Brazilian heavy rare-earth producer Serra Verde via USA Rare Earth, but both deals rest on contested legal authority in the US, Venezuela and Brazil. Monica de Bolle argues the resulting resource 'wins' are fragile and may last no longer than Trump's time in office, with Brazil's new critical minerals law and the October election as the near-term reversal risk.

insights.claim: The Pentagon directed $750 million into a special purpose vehicle to fund USA Rare Earth, which holds a 15-year agreement for mixed rare earth carbonate from Brazilian miner Serra Verde, with the US government holding a 10 percent equity stake in Serra Verde after USA Rare Earth acquired it.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: US sovereign capital is now directly on the cap table of a foreign rare-earth miner; track USA Rare Earth's offtake economics and the Pentagon's guaranteed-price commitments as a template for future critical-minerals financing.
insights.quote: the Pentagon directed $750 million into a special purpose vehicle to fund USA Rare Earth, which holds a 15-year agreement for mixed rare earth carbonate from Brazilian mining company Serra Verde
insights.locator: Around the same time the Venezuelan oil deal

insights.claim: Both the Brazilian minerals deal and the Venezuelan oil deal run through Pentagon industrial-policy mechanisms — the Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment (IBAS) program for Brazil and the Office of Strategic Capital for Venezuela — each combining an equity-like stake with a long-term offtake agreement at a guaranteed price governed by US law.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: The equity-plus-guaranteed-price-offtake structure is the repeatable US playbook for strategic resources; suppliers able to fit that template can capture subsidized capital and price floors.
insights.quote: Both would take an equity-like stake in addition to a long-term offtake agreement at a guaranteed price, governed by US law.
insights.locator: Pentagon involvement in both deals

insights.claim: The stated rationale for routing resource investments through the Pentagon is to displace Chinese and Russian operators from accessing Latin American resources, framing commercial mining and oil stakes as defense policy.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Expect more defense-budget money to flow into upstream resource assets wherever Chinese offtake is currently dominant.
insights.locator: The rationale for invoking the Pentagon

insights.claim: The 15-year Serra Verde offtake agreement was placed in a special purpose vehicle rather than at the Pentagon itself presumably because the IBAS statute caps purchase commitments at 10 years and does not directly mention equity.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: The SPV structure is a workaround for a statutory limit, which is precisely the seam a future Congress or administration could attack to unwind the investment.
insights.locator: In Brazil, the statute governing IBAS

themes.theme: Legal fragility on the US side

insights.claim: The Office of Strategic Capital was created in 2022 to issue loans and loan guarantees, and Congress has so far declined to grant it authority to hold equity stakes, leaving the legal basis of the Pentagon's equity positions unsettled.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: An unauthorized-equity challenge is a live tail risk for any company whose valuation depends on a Pentagon stake or guaranteed offtake.
insights.quote: Congress has thus far declined to grant it any authority to hold equity stakes, and this issue remains unsettled.
insights.locator: The legal foundations in the United States are not clearly settled

insights.claim: Trump used executive order authority to permit critical minerals investments including those in USA Rare Earth, removing them from routine congressional review.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Deals resting on executive orders rather than statute can be reversed by the stroke of a successor's pen — duration risk is political, not contractual.
insights.locator: President Trump, however, used his executive order authority

insights.claim: The Pentagon's authority to fund the Venezuela oil deal expires in 2028 even though its commitments in Venezuela run for 100 years, a mismatch of roughly two years of authority against a century of obligation.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: The funding cliff in 2028 is a concrete, datable catalyst for the deal's unwinding or renegotiation.
insights.quote: The Pentagon's authority to fund Venezuela's oil deal expires in 2028, even though its commitments in Venezuela run for 100 years.
insights.locator: The Pentagon's authority to fund Venezuela's oil deal

insights.claim: Placing the contracts under US law does not solve enforcement risk, because US courts can only enforce a contract if the signing parties had the legitimacy and power to sign it — which the Venezuelan interim government lacks and which the Pentagon arguably lacks on the equity side.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: The standard 'governed by New York law' comfort that investors price in is illusory here; counterparty legitimacy, not jurisdiction, is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: But US courts can enforce a contract only if the parties involved had the legitimacy and power to sign it in the first place.

themes.theme: Brazil election and the new minerals law

insights.claim: Lula tried to block the USA Rare Earth acquisition of Serra Verde but was thwarted because the transaction was found compliant with existing Brazilian law, exposing that Brazil lacked an adequate screening regime for foreign concessions.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: The screening gap that let this deal through is now being closed, so the window for similar acquisitions of Brazilian mineral assets is shutting.
insights.locator: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva tried to block the deal

insights.claim: Lula fast-tracked a bill establishing new rules for critical minerals projects that the Brazilian Congress approved on September 2, 2026, creating a legal mechanism a future government could use to review or negate the Serra Verde transaction.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Enactment of this law is the specific trigger to watch for a post-election challenge to foreign ownership of Brazilian rare-earth assets.
insights.locator: In response, Lula fast-tracked a bill

insights.claim: Brazil's October presidential race is very close, and the outcome is the pivotal variable: a re-elected Lula would likely wield the new critical minerals law to revisit the Serra Verde deal, whereas Flávio Bolsonaro — who has Trump's implicit endorsement — would likely try to honor it.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Brazil's October election is a binary event for the ownership and offtake rights of the only large-scale non-Asian heavy rare-earth supply; position sizing in that supply chain should reflect it.
insights.locator: If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected in October

insights.claim: The Serra Verde deal has become active campaign material for Lula, whose re-election bid is premised on protecting Brazilian economic sovereignty.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Resource nationalism has become an electoral asset in Brazil, raising the political cost of any further foreign acquisition of strategic mineral assets.
insights.quote: His campaign, after all, is premised on protecting Brazilian economic sovereignty.
insights.locator: As Lula discovered, the Serra Verde deal

insights.claim: The August oil deal gives the United States access to about 20 percent of proven Venezuelan oil reserves, secured by an interim government under Delcy Rodríguez that is widely viewed as a puppet regime installed after Maduro was seized and jailed in Brooklyn on narcotics-trafficking charges.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: A fifth of Venezuela's proven reserves theoretically entering US-controlled hands is a major long-run supply variable, but only if the concession survives its legitimacy problem.
insights.locator: The extraordinary oil deal with Venezuela forged in August

insights.claim: The US Department of Defense took an equity stake in a private oil venture controlled by Venezuelan billionaire Alejandro Betancourt, who has faced money-laundering charges brought by the United States and Switzerland.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Counterparty and reputational risk is embedded at the operating level, adding a sanctions/legal-challenge vector on top of the sovereignty risk.
insights.locator: The Venezuelan oil deal has been widely criticized

insights.claim: The Venezuela arrangement grants a 100-year concession under majority foreign control, terms that appear forbidden by the Venezuelan constitution even though enforcement is currently impossible because the country's institutions have been dismantled.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Unenforceable today does not mean unenforceable later; the constitutional defect is a dormant claim that reactivates whenever Venezuelan institutions are rebuilt.
insights.quote: the deal grants a 100-year concession under majority foreign control. These terms appear to be forbidden by the Venezuelan constitution
insights.locator: These deals lack clear legal authority

insights.claim: A future Venezuelan government arising from an actual election would likely challenge the concessions and push the dispute into arbitration, repeating the pattern of previous Venezuelan expropriations.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Expect years of arbitration claims rather than clean ownership; the realistic payoff profile resembles distressed legal claims, not producing reserves.
insights.locator: In Venezuela, a future government

insights.claim: Serra Verde is the first large-scale producer outside Asia capable of supplying heavy rare-earth elements needed for the high-performance magnets used in missile guidance systems and other weaponry.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: This single Brazilian asset is the scarcest link in Western heavy rare-earth supply, which is why political risk around it transmits directly to defense-magnet supply chains.
insights.quote: Serra Verde is the first large-scale producer outside Asia capable of supplying heavy rare-earth elements needed for high-performance magnets used in missile guidance systems and other weaponry.
insights.locator: Crucially, Serra Verde is the first large-scale producer

insights.claim: Genuinely securing strategic supply chains would have required clear US legal authority for the Pentagon to invest plus a binding host-country agreement that holds regardless of who is in power, and neither condition was met.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Use these two tests — domestic statutory authority and host-country durability — to screen any headline resource-security deal for whether it will actually deliver volumes.

insights.claim: Despite the rhetoric about securing Latin American resources at China's expense, the deals amount to a purchase that may last only as long as Trump is in power and likely won't deliver anything by the time he leaves office.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Fade the narrative that US supply-chain independence in heavy rare earths or Venezuelan oil has been achieved; physical delivery timelines exceed the political durability of the arrangements.
insights.quote: all Trump has achieved is a purchase that may last only as long as he is in power and likely won't deliver anything by the time he leaves
insights.locator: For all the noise about securing Latin American resources

insights.claim: Political risk is baked into both the Brazil and Venezuela deals because of Latin America's long history of changing governments abrogating deals with US corporations and sometimes seizing assets without compensation.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Discount rates on these assets should reflect expropriation history rather than the guaranteed-price offtake terms on paper.
insights.quote: In other words, political risk is baked into both of these deals.
insights.locator: The deals with Venezuela and Brazil both come at a pivotal moment

insights.claim: The Serra Verde transaction received far less attention and publicity than the Venezuelan oil deal despite following the same template of US government-linked ownership of a foreign strategic resource producer.
insights.speaker: Monica de Bolle
insights.so_what: Underfollowed deals carry mispriced political risk; the Brazil leg is the less-crowded expression of the same trade.
insights.quote: Much less attention and publicity have been accorded to a similar deal with Brazil
insights.locator: The extraordinary oil deal with Venezuela forged in August
